desc:
When Someone Doesn't Want You in Their Life Anymore, They Show These 7 Signs

Almost nobody announces that they are done with you. There is no conversation, no final word, no clean ending you can point to later. Instead there are seven small changes, and every one of them is easy to explain away on its own. That is exactly why people stay for another year, collecting explanations. By the end of this video you will be able to count them honestly, and the sixth one predicts the ending better than everything else on this list combined.

📌 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:
✓ Why short replies are a measurement and not a mood
✓ The eighty six percent finding about small bids for attention
✓ Why the end of the fighting is worse news than the fighting
✓ How closeness runs backwards on the way out
✓ What happens to the word we
✓ The one sign that predicts the ending better than any other
✓ The single question that settles it in ten seconds

⏱️ CHAPTERS:
0:00 Intro
0:50 The Replies
1:32 The Bids
2:27 No Fighting
3:30 Reverse
4:10 The Word
4:54 Contempt
6:16 The Question
6:42 Close

🧠 THE SCIENCE:
John Gottman observed couples in a research apartment and tracked what he called bids for connection, the small moments when one person reaches for attention. Couples who were still together six years later had turned toward those bids about eighty six percent of the time. Couples who separated had turned toward them about thirty three percent of the time. Gottman also identified contempt, the expression of superiority toward a partner, as the strongest single predictor of relationship breakdown. Altman and Taylor described social penetration theory, showing that closeness builds through widening self disclosure, which means it also visibly narrows on the way out. And research on pronoun use by Seider and colleagues found that couples who used we language showed better outcomes than those who shifted toward I and you.

💡 KEY TAKEAWAY:
Stop auditioning for a role in a life that has already been cast.

📚 RESEARCH MENTIONED:
• Gottman, J. M., & DeClaire, J. (2001). The Relationship Cure. Crown.
• Gottman, J. M., & Silver, N. (1999). The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work. Crown.
• Altman, I., & Taylor, D. A. (1973). Social Penetration: The Development of Interpersonal Relationships. Holt, Rinehart and Winston.
• Seider, B. H., Hirschberger, G., Nelson, K. L., & Levenson, R. W. (2009). We can work it out: Age differences in relational pronouns, physiology, and behavior in marital conflict. Psychology and Aging.

This video is for education and self-reflection. It is not therapy or relationship counseling.

🔔 Subscribe to Unchased for the psychology of men who stopped chasing.
